text_fidelity_a:
Arlo VMS5140-100NAS Ultra - 4K UHD Wire-Free Security 1 Camera System Update: one star. Stopped holding a charge after 3 months.

These are the first security cameras we've ever used, and I was able to install them myself in about a half hour. While they do a good job recording video and saving it so I can view it on my phone, the app is lacking and there are a couple of things that I find frustrating. I'll break my review into pros and cons.

Pros:
1. Fast install
2. Rechargeable (but only one base station)
3. Can view what is going on in my house when I am not there, can talk to the dog if I see him getting into the trash
4. Backs up my videos so I can look at them later if I am not home but cannot check the notification
5. I like the option to have a light come on at night, sound a siren, or call emergency services.
6. Decent video, I don't think it's 4k HD though, and wonderful audio.

Cons
1. The battery life. It lasts about 5 days, but one of mine is mounted outside so I have to stand on a chair or ladder to disconnect it and reconnect it.
2. Only one charing base is included for two cameras. They usually die around the same time and I can only charge one, the extra chargers are pricey and it seems to be a proprietary wire.
3. It came with one magnetic mount, which I love, and another mount that is a screw and ball. This mount doesn't feel as secure and I don't get why it just didn't have two of the same ones. It looks weird having the same camera with different mounts.
3. They are 4k, IF you pay. If you don't then they record in a lower quality. I don't mind, but it's misleading how it's phrased.
4. The app is clunky. I found it hard to block out areas where I didn't need notifications (like, every car that drives by on the road). I also was overwhelmed with notifications every time someone walks through my living room. I figured out how to set the cameras to a schedule/geo-fence, but WATCH OUT! The geo-fence doesn't work if you disconnect your phone from Wifi when you leave.
5. Notifications: When I'm not home I get an alert every time my cats walk through the room, so I had to shut off notifications all together. A little frustrating, but understandable.
6. Timers. If you want the camera to run from 10pm to 5am, you have to set it for the current day 10pm-11:59 pm, then the next day from 12:01am to 5:00am. It's kind of difficult and it kept not saving it when I set it up that way so I gave up and just set it from 12:01am-5:00am.
text_fidelity_b: Arlo VMS5140-100NAS Ultra - 4K UHD Wire-Free Security 1 Camera System

text_fidelity_a:
JVC Soft Wireless Earbud with Stayfit Tips, Remote and Mic and Bluetooth Violet (HA-FX9BTV) 3.5 stars taking price into account

With headphones, it is always a blend of "you get what you paid for", and comparing to others at a similar price point.
How do these compare? Well, they are about average for the $20-$40 range. Not much better, not much worse. And as is the case with headphones, for a bit more, you can do MUCH better, and for a bit less, you will get roughly similar results. (In other words, headphones under $75-$100 are, more or less very similar, and then suddenly, your options get drastically better.)

Here's my analysis on the general sound quality and other features:

MISC:
Phone calls: 5 stars: Easy to use, works great for calls on both ends, and blocks outside sound quite well!
Ease of use/pairing: 5 stars: It passed the test of not having to read instructions, meaning it is incredibly simple to pair and use
Appearance: 5 stars: Neat! It's colorful and fun, as well as practical and functional!
External noise: 4 stars: Because it has a pretty tight seal, it is like an earplug, blocking outside sound quite effectively
Comfort: 3 stars: comparable to others of this design. Totally fine at first, and annoying after long use.

SOUND:
Treble: 2 stars: quite tinny
Bass: 2 stars: ok depth, not great, not very powerful
Overall: 2 stars: not much detail in the sound, but it can get pretty loud without distorting, and it is definitely good enough for basic listening and phone calls. There also appears to be a *very slight* hiss in quiet/silent moments when the volume is louder.

OVERALL:
The average is 28 out of 40 possible points, or 70% (a "C" grade, if it were going to school ;-), but because the above analysis does not take price point into account, comparing this to brands like Bose, as well as dollar store headphones, this means that for the current list price of roughly $29.99, this is a reasonable expectation.

The average number of stars based on my rubric is 3.5 stars: decent for this price point, and certainly good enough to enjoy music and spoken word, and to have successful phone calls.
text_fidelity_b: JVC Soft Wireless Earbud with Stayfit Tips, Remote and Mic and Bluetooth Violet (HA-FX9BTV)

text_fidelity_a:
iHome IHM28W2 Color Changing Alarm Clock FM Radio with USB Charging The home is a decent little alarm clock/speaker, though not always the finest in terms of design.

What does it do?
Acts as an alarm. Some people I noted were annoyed that you had to cycle through the minutes to set the time and alarm and while an hour button is easier, if you hold down the button it really zips through pretty quickly. In other words, you really don't have to plod through minute by minute. To give a sense of that, it took me 10 seconds to speed from 6:00 am to 10:00 am. So really, this isn't much of an issue in my mind. It has two alarms, which is a nice touch. The alarm can go to either the radio or to your input device, though that is a bit iffy depending on your device. It worked with my ipod touch but you're going to want to make sure your device works as it should. One problem is that it is not very easy to see in the dark.

Acts as a radio: the reception was quite good; I had no trouble with local stations. All tuned in well.

Acts as a speaker: the sound is decent for what it is. It certainly isn't going to replace your stereo or even a set of decent bluetooth speakers, but that isn't really its goal and for what it's meant to do, and what its probably target audience is (children, tweens, young teen) I'm sure it's fine.

Work with audio devices--this is a bit mixed. I've had variability with a range of Apple products. They all work in terms of producing sound, but the volume varied amongst them at times so that even with the volume all the way up on both devices it was surprisingly low. Not inaudible or anything, but not loud enough for good entertainment (probably OK for an alarm). You also just basically sit your device atop between two plastic "walls"--there's no cradle or anything and so there isn't much difference between that and just lying it flat next to or atop it. It charged my devices, but it's not a charging cradle, which would have been nicer. Instead there is a USB charge slot on the bottom of the device and you use your own charging cable. The same is true for the audio--you use a cable jack into your device (this one is provided) to link the two. It's an adequate design, if not an elegant one.

Glow/change colors: Well, it does do this. My response? Meh. But then, again, I'm really not I'm assuming the target audience. It doesn't do a anything for me, but kids and tweens might find it interesting. At the least, it isn't obnoxious (not too bright, not too fast-changing, etc.)

it's plastic, but it feels pretty hefty and the build seems decent if a little cheap. I certainly didn't have the sense that it would be fragile or break down soon or anything.

in the end, I'd say it's a decent little device for a tween sort. Not sure it's worth 50 dollars, but it's not exorbitant, just maybe a little pricey. If you're just looking for a speaker, I'd say there are bluetooth ones out there that provide better sound for the price. But if you want a speaker/alarm/radio/something to look at now and then, it's a decent purchase.
text_fidelity_b: iHome IHM28W2 Color Changing Alarm Clock FM Radio with USB Charging

text_fidelity_a:
NEW Microsoft Surface Headphones 2 - Light Gray I'm not an audiophile, but I've tried out a good number of different earbud brands lately, all across the quality spectrum. I'm grading on a curve here.

Packaging is sufficient. A few tip sizes, quick start, instructions, and whatever is in that other manual of junk I always throw away. The earbud case is lozenge shaped and pocketable enough. No external lights, which is nice if you're charging it next to your bed, but not so much if you want to know their charge status.

They are supposed to immediately start trying to bluetooth pair with something when first opened, and appeared to be trying to do so. My Surface was unable to locate them. I even tried with a second Surface. I plugged in the case and left it to charge for 15 minutes, and then they paired fine. Overall on unboxing and setup, I'd say they're adequate, but far from exceptional.

The earbuds themselves are aggressively visible. I assume they're trying to ride the I-Pod branding success, but I'm not really feeling it. Despite looking huge, they don't feel huge. They are lightweight and comfortable. They don't feel like they are going to fall out, despite not feeling like they're crammed in the ear. Fit is unusual in that you can turn the earbud like a screw to make it tighter or looser. Sound is good. I'm giving them very low marks for appearance, and very good for fit and sound.

These use swipe style controls, which I despise. I much prefer a physical button that I can just feel that I've clicked. The controls do work as advertised, but there's enough delay that it often takes me a while of swiping my ear and waiting until it gets the message. Mostly irritating when someone tries to talk to me and I can't get it to pause for several seconds.

Range is average.

Overall, Id' say there's a bit of a brand name premium on the price compared to some other products, and I'm saying that as someone who has used Surface products as my primary computers for many years now, but they're not bad. I've definitely tried more expensive earbuds that weren't as good, but of what I've tried, I'm happiest so far with the Jabra Elite series of earbuds.

text_fidelity_a:
GAOMON PD2200 130% sRGB Full-Laminated Pen Display with 8192 Battery-Free Tilt-Support Stylus 8 Touch Buttons -21.5'' Graphics Drawing Tablet Monitor with Adjustable Stand I am a huge supporter of open source graphics software because I feel that the leading brand name software uses their virtual monopoly to bully people into overpriced, restrictive, nonsensical subscription programs. When I saw that this tablet was listed as being compatible with GIMP and most other graphics programs, I felt comfortable purchasing it for my uses.

However, upon installing it, I found that it is not actually compatible with the vast majority of graphic software except for those supported by Adobe, and a couple of other inferior programs. To clarify, it will still "function" with most programs, but only as a basic mouse. It will not support pressure sensitivity nor tilt. This, in my mind, means that it is NOT compatible, as pressure and tilt are essential functions for any illustrator. Without them, this is basically just a glorified mouse pad.

From Gaomon's troubleshooting website regarding lack of pressure sensitivity:

"The version of your drawing program might be too low to support pen pressure. Please upload it or try to draw in other drawing programs. Here do we suggest you some drawing programs. For windows system: Adobe Photoshop CC, Adobe Photoshop CC 2015, Adobe Photoshop CC 2017, Adobe Photoshop CC 2018, Adobe Photoshop cs5，Adobe Photoshop cs6, Adobe Animate CC2017 For Mac system: Adobe Photoshop CC, Adobe Photoshop CC 2015, Adobe Photoshop CC 2017, Adobe Photoshop cs5, Adobe Photoshop cs6, Adobe illustrator cs6, Adobe Flash Professional CC, Adobe Animate CC 2018 Other free drawing programs: Sai, Krita, FireAlpaca"

Contrast that with the information in the product listing, which says, "compatible with most of major drawing software such as Photoshop、SAI version 2、Illustrator、krita、firealpaca、gimp、SketchBook Pro、MediBang Paint Pro, etc."

GIMP and others are clearly listed, but are not actually compatible. This is highly misleading.

As for other aspects of the tablet, I can't say too much as I haven't used it very much due to this issue. However, from what I have found so far, the display looks good, and the set up is pretty straightforward, although their manual is extremely confusing to try to follow.

The buttons on the side of the display are completely smooth and can not be felt; there is nothing there to help you locate them by tactile means, so you will have to stop looking at your work and visually find them in order to use them. They are also located such that they are easily pressed accidentally when adjusting the position of your tablet, which gets annoying pretty quickly.

The chords that come with the tablet are a bit short, maybe 4 or 5 feet, which doesn't allow for much room to position your tablet if you use a PC that is located beneath your desk or to the side, especially if the hook-up ports are on the back of the PC. You can of course buy replacement chords.

The stylus is very lightweight, which I personally consider a positive but some people may prefer a heftier stylus.

There is not much lag when using the stylus; the movement is smooth enough for my needs. The pressure sensitivity, when tested in a diagnostic program, seems quite good as well. It just doesn't work with the software I hoped to use it with.

Overall the tablet is a nice size and has a nice display, but the other issues are factors you should consider when deciding between this tablet and a more expensive brand.
text_fidelity_b: GAOMON PD2200 130% sRGB Full-Laminated Pen Display with 8192 Battery-Free Tilt-Support Stylus 8 Touch Buttons -21.5'' Graphics Drawing Tablet Monitor with Adjustable Stand

text_fidelity_a:
Turtle Beach Recon 70 Multiplatform Gaming Headset for Xbox Series X| S, Xbox One, PS5, PS4, PlayStation, Nintendo Switch, Mobile, & PC with 3.5mm-Flip-to-Mute Mic, 40mm Speakers-Blue Camo I got these for my 7yr old who kept wanting to use my Sennheiser's. After about the fourth time he dropped them and/or tried to walk off with them still on his head I decided it was time for kiddo to get his own headset. I was skeptical of these, due to the low price, but the reviews were decent.. and he's a menace, so figured I'd see.

Pros:
*Price, they are wonderfully priced for what they provide
*Mic is crystal clear, his voice comes across bit higher pitched but he's 7 its not like it was all that low to begin with.
*Flip up mic to mute. I love this feature, I have it on my Senn's and I'm not sure I could do with out it. If you hate push to talk, then you want a flip to mute mic. Unless you like to entertain discord with your drama.
*They are adjustable to the point that both my kid and my husband fit them comfortably.
*Volume adjust is on the earpiece, I hate trying to find it on the cord, this is much more convenient. Now I just have to convince him that he needs to keep the volume at a safe low level. His headphones for school are for kids and had a volume limiter. I see why now.

Cons:
*The connector cable is old school rubberized plastic (rather than the more durable braided cord).
*Connector is also super short, no way he is using them on a docked Switch
*They feel a bit flimsy and plastic, however this also makes the light which is nice
*Thin on the padding across the headpiece, although the ear cups are comfortable enough
*Ear cups are on the smaller size. They were fine for everyone in our household, but if you have issues with headsets and your ears you will probably have them with this set.

As a neither pro or con, these only block some outside sound. I wouldn't say they are open or close, but somewhere in between. He can still hear me yell at him from the other room which is nice, but I do have to yell. Sound is lacking in substantial bass, but at this price they are all going to be. For a gaming headset under $50, the sound is crisp and clear, as was the mic.

TL;DR If you are on a budget or just don't want to see an expensive pair get destroyed (kids, dogs, etc) I highly recommend these. I did ding a star though for the cord, they say they are for the Switch and I just don't see how a docked switch could use these.
text_fidelity_b: Turtle Beach Recon 70 Multiplatform Gaming Headset for Xbox Series X| S, Xbox One, PS5, PS4, PlayStation, Nintendo Switch, Mobile, & PC with 3.5mm-Flip-to-Mute Mic, 40mm Speakers-Blue Camo

text_fidelity_a:
Coby Kyros 7-Inch Android 2.3 4 GB Internet Touchscreen Tablet - MID7012-4G (Black) I never owned a tablet or a smartphone so I suppose if I did my review might be different but I think this is a pretty neat little tablet and the price is pretty great too.

I've had it for a couple of days and downloaded the Amazon App store which has most of the apps anyone could need. I mean seriously how many apps does an average person really use? I have downloaded quite a few games for both myself and my kids, the Kindle app, I heart Radio app, and the US newspaper app. So far its holding all of it but I also ordered a microsdhc card for extra space to hold more apps and e-books. I have a regular Kindle that I've had for quite a few years and I am able to transfer most of the books onto this tablet also (I haven't tried downloading all of them since my son uses a few for school). It has where you can calibrate the stylus. Also if you longpress the stylus onto the wallpaper it will let you change the wallpaper in the background.

It does not come with a camera and flashplayer is not installed (but what I understand you can install a "lite" version of flashplayer which I have not done as of yet). The touchscreen is more geared toward using the stylus (which is included) which is a let down to some people. You can use your fingertip but it isn't as responsive as with the stylus IMO. It also comes with a sleeve (that has a place for your stylus) and earphones. There is a charger and a USB cable. There is another cable which I'm not sure exactly what its for (sorry). I haven't used the other cables just yet (except the charger of course). As for battery life it does seem like it runs down pretty quickly (perhaps 3-4 hours). Of course, that may change depending on the type of apps you have running. I know a lot of people worry about reading books from this rather than the Kindle type e-ink. I, personally, like reading at night before I go to sleep and with the Kindle I had to keep a lamp on just to see the page..(barely)...whereas this isn't like that (my eyes are much happier!) You can change the brightness of the screen if you are worried about the brightness bothering your eyes.

I have my email accessible to the Coby Kyros so I can check it throughout the day since my daughter takes off with my laptop quite often. I also downloaded the Dolphin mini browser which I like better than the browser sent with the Kyros. It comes with the GetJar app store which has quite a few apps but Amazon has more.

Of course, I cannot guarantee how well it will hold up because I've only had it for a couple of days but overall its a nice simple little tablet. I've seen the reviews of more expensive tablets and I don't want to spend $400 on a tablet that's rated two stars. I was willing to take the chance and so far I'm happy with my purchase. I rated it 4 stars because the speaker is kinda crappy...I haven't tried listening to the radio with earphones...hopefully it sounds better. And also I wish that it was easier to install flash (I've been looking on the internet but it seems like you have to be really a techie to do it...and I'm not!) It's not an Ipad (or Ipod) so you can't rate this tablet against a product like that (of course it's half the price of a Ipod touch).
text_fidelity_b: Coby Kyros 7-Inch Android 2.3 4 GB Internet Touchscreen Tablet - MID7012-4G (Black)

Sony 16GB Microvault USB Flash Drive for Smartphone (USM16SA1/B) After reading the comments here, I decided to not bother with the Sony software. I installed "Nexus Media Importer" from the Google Android app store and it automatically detects and mounts the Sony device. I can read and write files with no problem, including playing audio and video files without copying them to the phone memory. On my PC, the Sony device mounts like any other flash drive. I would give this 5 stars if it was $30 (and if it came with better instructions), but the $45 price seems high for what is essentially a flash drive with a micro-USB port. You can get the same functionality (in a larger form factor) by using a regular flash drive and an OTG cable (sold here on Amazon for less than $2).

EDIT: I'm still happy with this device, but since writing this review, I've noticed that several other companies (SanDisk and others) have come out with similar products (flash drives with both micro and regular USB connectors) and some of them have much faster USB3.0 speeds. Sony has reduced their price to be competitive. Shop around; I expect functionality is similar.
text_fidelity_b: Sony 16GB Microvault USB Flash Drive for Smartphone (USM16SA1/B)

text_fidelity_a:
FYHXele Computer Monitor, Gaming Monitor 24 Inch 75Hz, IPS FHD 1080P, 2xHDMI, USB Type-C, Built-in Speakers, Adaptive Sync, VESA for Office Home, Black I’ve been using the FYHXele 24 Inch Monitor (75Hz version) for the last month, and it has totally spoiled me for playing games on my Switch! The monitor has built-in speakers, so I can hear a game’s music while playing. It’s a small but nice feature; I can easily switch the input from my laptop to my Switch and not have to rearrange my whole desk to play games.

The picture is bright and vibrant. I’ve been playing Hades for the last month and it looks SO good on this screen. Bright and crisp, even if I play during the day. I also use the monitor as a second display for work, it’s good for that too, either as a streaming display or for text and spreadsheets.

I use it with my MacBook Pro, the monitor has 2 HDMI inputs and 1 USB-C. The USB-C port doesn’t support passthrough charging.

A VESA plate is included, which was a nice plus. I do use a monitor arm because I don’t like the stand this monitor comes with. The angle and height are not adjustable at all, and I didn’t like the default angle. The base is 9 inches by 7 inches, so it has a large footprint. I also don’t love the “FYHXele” printed in white at the bottom of the screen.

The power cable is relatively short, only 50 inches. It’s an AC adapter, not a power brick. The box also includes an HDMI cable -- another nice plus -- but unfortunately my cable had a cut in the coating, so I could see the copper wire.

Overall, I think this is a decent budget monitor. I never want to play my Switch in handheld mode anymore, the picture quality has spoiled me that much. The dual HDMI inputs make it easy to switch between work and fun; I’ve also used this as a Discord display, rotated 90° on a VESA arm.
text_fidelity_b: FYHXele Computer Monitor, Gaming Monitor 24 Inch 75Hz, IPS FHD 1080P, 2xHDMI, USB Type-C, Built-in Speakers, Adaptive Sync, VESA for Office Home, Black

text_fidelity_a:
Fire Tablet with Alexa, 7" Display, 16 GB, Blue - with Special Offers (Previous Generation - 5th) My top ten include dogs, sewing machines, houses, my bed, a few trips, and my Kindle. I love my Kindle so much that I actually bought a Kindle edition of a big, heavy, expensive book that I have in hardback just so I don't have to carry it around. It has taken just one month for me to only want to read with the Kindle. It's going to save lots of bookshelf space, my bookshelves are jammed. I love being able to use the dictionary and look up many more words than I used to. Yes, you know the meaning from the context, but it's fun to know the etymology. I took Latin many years ago and frequently consider the root meanings of words, and having the Kindle dictionary makes this easier. Wikipedia is wonderful, too. I looked up the Magna Charta while I was reading a book that mentioned it, and found when it was written, what it was about, etc. I have also looked up some cities to find demographic and weather information.
The ability to change font size and page justification is a good feature. It is important to realize, however, that you can't change justification if the book wasn't formatted to allow that. You get those giant gaps on some lines when it's in full justification. If you use a small font, it's not so bad. Most of the books I have purchased allow left justification, and my guess is that more and more books will be formatted that way, which generally eliminates those gaps. You can get the first chapters of books as free samples, and see how they are formatted, as well as whether you like them as far as writing and subject is concerned.
The next thing I plan to do is put some of my music from my iPod onto the Kindle so I can listen to background music while I read. I understand you can't control the order of the songs, so I'm only going to put on classical music that is not distracting in and of itself.
Getting more books fast is great, too. I forget the name for the phobia that is the fear of running out of things to read, but I have a small case of that, and Kindle is the cure.
Traveling is much nicer when you don't have ten books in your book bag.
I'm asking for an SD card for Christmas from one of the grandkids (it's very inexpensive) so that the Kindle will have even greater capacity.
When you go to the Kindle store from your Kindle, there will be recommendations based on what you have bought, just like there are when you go to Amazon online. However, online you can say "not interested," but on the Kindle, you can't. You get the same recommendations over and over. It would be nice if you could delete recommendations from your Kindle. But, hey, that is definitely just a small thing.
Another thing that would be nice is a password for 1-click ordering from the Kindle.
I'm retired and on a relatively small income. If I lost my Kindle and couldn't afford another one, I would go back to work just long enough to get the money to replace it. That should tell you how much I love it, 'cause I sure don't want to work anymore!
text_fidelity_b: Fire Tablet with Alexa, 7" Display, 16 GB, Blue - with Special Offers (Previous Generation - 5th)

text_fidelity_a:
BAOFENG BF-F8HP (UV-5R 3rd Gen) 8-Watt Dual Band Two-Way Radio (136-174MHz VHF & 400-520MHz UHF) Includes Full Kit with Large Battery Received as a Christmas gift. As I am not a licensed ham yet I have not transmitted on the radio, so I can't speak about any transmission issues that others may have experienced. To date I have only used it to monitor ham radio bands to understand how hams communicate.

For an affordable introductory ham radio, Baofeng radios are a good choice. Some ham "purists" seem to have nothing good to say about them, but many hams are welcoming of new operators and understand that these radios have the potential to expand the hobby.

The radio comes with a decent book (when ordered from BAOFENG TECH). There are also quite a few resources and videos online to assist in usage.

I found programming of stations to be fairly simple although a bit time consuming. There isn't really that much to it. If you are going to program in multiple channels or set offsets for repeater use then a programming cable would be a good investment. The programming cable also allows you to name individual channels.

There are some potential issues that can occur with use of this radio.

1. This radio covers VHF and UHF ham bands but also conflicts with police bands, city maintenance, and private corporation radio frequencies. There is the potential to accidentally transmit on an unauthorized band.

2. While this radio will scan UHF/VHF police, fire and EMT bands most have shifted to a new system. Some agencies are on the older systems and some simulcast on UHF/VHF but in general if you are planning on using this as a police scanner you probably aren't going to hear much.

3. There is no way to lock out the transmit key, so it is easy to press it while handling the radio if not paying attention.

As a monitoring radio the battery seems to last forever. If you are planning on transmitting a lot then an extra battery or 12VDC adapter may be warranted.

So far I really don't have anything negative to say. Good introductory radio.
text_fidelity_b: BAOFENG BF-F8HP (UV-5R 3rd Gen) 8-Watt Dual Band Two-Way Radio (136-174MHz VHF & 400-520MHz UHF) Includes Full Kit with Large Battery

TCL 75R617 - 75-Inch 4K Ultra HD Roku Smart LED TV (2019 Model) with TCL TS5010 - Alto 5+ 2.1 Channel Home Theater Sound Bar with Wireless Subwoofer I needed an upgrade; my 9 year old Vizio was not cutting it any more. Reading the reviews I decided on the TCL 55r615. The voice remote on the r617 wasn’t worth the extra fifty bucks, and the voice function is duplicated on the Roku phone app anyway.

I am VERY happy with the TV; Colors and picture are bright and contrast seems excellent. I’ve watched a couple of 4k documentaries and was blown away with the picture. The Roku menu for the streaming channels really is excellent to use: Far “Snappier” and easier to navigate than any other that I’ve used. (Including my Sony Blu-ray player) The Roku set up allows setting up the apps on your PC and updating the TV afterwards making initial set up a breeze. The Roku app allows listening with headphones to whatever is on the TV, but I haven’t used that yet. (I read where people have purchased older Roku remotes that have the headphone jack, but don’t need that function myself)

Since I read that many people had problems with Banding, I downloaded some test JPG’s to a thumb drive and tested the set: It passed! No banding was seen and colors were even with the exception of very slight darkening in the four corners. Even knowing it’s there, I can’t see it on live TV so I’m happy.

The bad parts: the screen is more reflective than my old set. Since I was going to wall mount the set anyways, I’ll point the screen downwards to minimize the glare. I’m certain the high end TVs costing 4 times as much have this covered, but I’m good with my TCL. Setting up my Directv remote to the set was a HUGE PITA. This was more a problem with the remote than the TCL set, but was an hour of my life I want back.

I haven’t tried using a sound bar with the ARC/CEC function, but I don’t anticipate any issues. Overall, I’m pleased to have found such high quality at this price-point and would recommend this set.
text_fidelity_b: TCL 75R617 - 75-Inch 4K Ultra HD Roku Smart LED TV (2019 Model) with TCL TS5010 - Alto 5+ 2.1 Channel Home Theater Sound Bar with Wireless Subwoofer

And granted they are only 35 ohm I have it on good authority that they will drive the big boys with out breaking a sweat. The only gripe I have is the battery life. I only run 2.5mm balanced so the battery usually taps out after about 5-6 hours. Not bad, but not the ES100’s 10 hours. But the power, man this sucker punches way above it’s weight. I use it mainly with my Samsung Galaxy phone and strictly LDAP. Everything else is disabled in the software/app that FiiO provides. And that is my second gripe. The ES100 rules on the app side. If FiiO put some time and money into providing similar functionality into their red headed stepchild app they could ask twice the price and I’d still think it was a bargain. But all the gripes aside it is definitely a step up from the ES100. Some told me if you have the Radsone that you’re good to go, no need to buy the FiiO. Fiddlesticks, BahHumbug and all those other quaking aphorisms. Buy it. It will make you smile.

text_fidelity_a:
FiiO X5 High Resolution Music Player (2nd Generation)(Titanium) I love my FiiO X5 2nd gen player! I love that it has two micro SD card slots (which I use both for a total of 192GB of storage space, with one 64GB card and one 128GB card), because I can put two separate sets of music in there and go back and forth between the cards depending on my musical needs (for example, on the 64GB card, I put recently purchased tracks, and for the entirety of my rest of my library, I put those tracks on the 128GB card). It allows me faster access to my newer stuff, which I want to listen to now, vs. randomizing the rest of my music from the other card.

The sound is unheard of (ha ha, sorry for the pun). Nothing compares to the quality of sound that comes out of this little machine, for its size and price. Pair it with a set of high quality hi-fi headphones and some FLAC music files, and you've got yourself an insane little music machine. You'll never go back to Apple or another brand of music player. You'll find yourself hooking it up to your home sound system and playing all of your music through it. I can't say enough for the sound quality. You WILL notice a difference between crummy .mp3 files and other low-quality sound files. You WILL find yourself craving FLAC files, and you will go wherever you can to find them. You might even start converting your entire CD music collection into FLAC, even though you'd already converted them all to .mp3. You WILL find yourself hoping that someday soon, Amazon will start offering FLAC files instead of .mp3s! (HINT HINT NUDGE NUDGE!) ;) Seriously, though, you probably haven't realized how GOOD your music will sound until you listen to it on this FiiO X5 2nd gen. Even the .mp3s sound better. Especially if you use noise cancelling headphones.

I like that you can adjust the configuration and tell it which buttons to remain active when the screen is off, depending on your preferences. I also like that there are several preset themes to choose from. The screen is easy to read and nicely displays album art.

The unit itself has a wonderful weight to it given the aluminum shell. The volume wheel moves easily and there is a slight tactile feedback click. That wheel controls both the song volume and song selection, depending on which screen you're on when you use it. The power on button has a tiny LED light that's blue when it's running and red when it's charging. There are volume up/down buttons beneath the power button and those buttons are some of the buttons that you can choose whether or not to have active while the screen is off.

I'm not sure if I there's a firmware update that needs to be done that could change this, but there are a couple of things that are pretty bothersome in general about this unit:

1) There is no way to search for a song. If, like me, you have more than 5,000 songs, it's impossible to sit and scroll through each album/folder to find a specific song. I suppose if you're some kind of major organization guru (which I thought I was, but apparently not at this), it would be possible to arrange your music folders into genres or some other category to make it easier to get to the exact music you need to play, but if you've moved over from iTunes like I have, you're probably real spoiled with the ability to view songs either by artist, album, song name, etc., as well as the ability to do a search. Here, you're pretty much on your own, depending on how you've got your music library set up. Having purchased most of my music here on Amazon, it's all arranged by artist name in individual folders. I have several hundred folders set up like this, and scrolling through everything with that scroll wheel can take a very, very long time to find the one thing you're looking for.

2) The unit can be quite SLOW to respond to your clicks. It is not touch-screen, and when you click on a button to change tracks forward/backward or to change from looking at what's playing into another option, such as a list of the songs on the album, it can be quite sluggish. Again, if you're used to using an iPod, you'll be frustrated with the lack of responsiveness of this unit. Again, I keep hoping a firmware update will come out that addresses this.

3) Whenever you add music to your micro SD card(s) [NOTE: There is NO onboard storage, it's purely on whatever card(s) you insert into it] you have to completely update your whole media library. This can take a long time depending on how much music you have, so keep this in mind and don't expect to add music and listen to it immediately. In other words, plan ahead for this :)

4) It's not as user friendly as the typical Apple products you may be used to. You'll get used to it, but don't expect the polished feel because of issues like #1 and #2, above.

5) Playlists are not straightforward. Yes, you can be playing a song and add it to a playlist that resides on one of your SD cards. However, importing playlists can be tricky and you may find yourself looking to the internet to help convert your existing playlists from your prior player. Expect to spend some time on this unless you're totally okay with starting over from scratch (I wasn't okay with this). Also, any playlists that you save to your SD card that you've hand-converted do not show up as a playlist on the FiiO. Instead, you have to navigate to the file on your player as if you were looking for a song, and play it as if you were playing a song. Only playlists you've created on the machine show up in the Playlist section, not playlists you've brought in from elsewhere. There is no 'import' feature or anything fancy like that, so you're pretty much on your own unless you add a song one at a time to Playlist 1, Playlist 2, etc. (I do not yet see a way to rename these as there is no keyboard function on this machine, so you're stuck with those names).

I think with time, the FiiO's software will catch up closer to what you're seeing from the high-visibility media consumer based music players, but right now with this X5 you should be more concerned with how WONDERFUL your music sounds vs the issues associated with the frumpy software that comes with it.
text_fidelity_b: FiiO X5 High Resolution Music Player (2nd Generation)(Titanium)

This UBS 3.1 cable is slower. If you look at the attached photos, the first is the drive with this cable and the 2nd is the exact same drive in the cheap USB 3.0 enclosure. Same computer. This is running the CrystalMark DiskMark 64S benchmarking tool, which is designed to effectively test SSDs.

Disappointing performance. On the plus side, it's certainly simpler to install (the Inatek requires 6 SMALL screws, which is kinda bonkers).
An SSD has no real need of the enclosure. So this seems like it would be a better solution. But not if speed matters.
The benchmark is automatically run 5x and I ran the whole thing twice because I expected this cable to be faster.

text_fidelity_a:
Blink Whole Home Bundle | Video Doorbell System, Outdoor camera, and Mini camera | HD video, motion detection, Works with Alexa "Set up in minutes"?? Not really. There are no actual detailed instructions included. I tried scanning the QR code that was provided in the little pamphlet, and that was not helpful. This ended up being extremely frustrating to set up. I could take a wild guess that I was supposed put the lithium batteries in the back of the camera. I would not have known that the little QR code inside the camera where the batteries go was something that I had to scan to set up the camera. Anyway, without going into detail, if Amazon provided some simple, basic instructions with photos that show step by step, it would save the customer a ton of fumbling around. Then it might have been an easy set up. I had to call for support, and by the time I got a support person on the phone I was pretty irritated. The reason I decided to buy this camera is the "two-year battery life." Note: these are not rechargeable batteries. We'll see how long the batteries last. Prior to this, I got a Eufy Solocam, also wireless (and much, much easier to set up), and it had rechargeable batteries advertised to last 4 months, but they lasted 4 weeks. A feature that is missing with the Blink camera, that I liked on the Eufy camera, is the AI feature to recognize humans. Without the AI feature, the Blink is recording non-human motion, such as animals and vehicles.

Update: The description advertises customized zones for motion detection. The camera takes a photo what it sees, and in motion settings, you gray out areas that you do not want the camera to detect motion. It does NOT work. I tried resetting it several times, and the camera recorded and sent me an alert of motion detected that was squarely in the grayed out area. Without this feature actually working, and without the AI feature to detect humans, the camera is recording every motion in the entire viewable area, ignoring the areas that I grayed out. I am returning this camera.
text_fidelity_b: Blink Whole Home Bundle | Video Doorbell System, Outdoor camera, and Mini camera | HD video, motion detection, Works with Alexa

text_fidelity_a:
Dzees 5W Solar Panel for Wireless Outdoor Security Camera, Compatible with Rechargeable Battery Powered Camera, Continuous Solar Power for Camera, Waterproof, Reliable and Non-Stop Green Charging This is the fourth camera from this company that I purchased and I have to say that I find the value to be overall a good deal. The main problem that I fine with them is when mounted outdoors they tend to fail after 2 to 3 months sometimes in other cases they last as long as a year but in every case they end up failing.

The really frustrating thing is that once they die there’s no way to bring them back and the battery life just doesn’t seem to last past a few months of outdoor abuse.

When paired with a solar charger they actually do quite well and are not problem to keep outside for Several weeks without charging.

The main drawback to this type of system is that it only records when there’s motion this is in order to save battery life and it has a small chip that does motion to Engage the camera once there’s actually motion going on.

Because of this many people are surprised that they can’t look at a point in time and see what was going on they have to only look at the motion events that are raised by the camera. All in all for a cheap and quick solution these were great if you need to monitor something critical I would look for another resource.

I think that's the next eclipse. These work great (hence four stars) but it's kind of a flawed idea.

They're too powerful. Maybe you can see some sunspots with these you'd miss with regular eclipse solar viewing glasses, but really the regular eclipse glasses work fine. I gave up on the binoculars and used those.

The fundamental problem with these is, how do you find the sun? It seems dumb, but at 8x, you spend a fair bit of time searching a perfectly black sky. You can't see anything through these EXCEPT the sun, so there are no landmarks or other things to guide you. Unless you peak at the sky and fry your eyeballs.

Plus, during the real show - totality - you can't use these at all. Nothing is visible.

VIDBOX Video Conversion Suite For years I've passed by expensive services offering to convert your old VHS tapes and 8 tracks to DVD. Thanks to this handy little device, there's no need for outside help - you can do it entirely on your own and save yourself lots of money.

Not only is this device easy to set up (if you've ever dubbed VHS tapes, it's roughly the same set-up) but it's compact (the device itself is the same size as a deck of cards). Unlike other gadgets these days, it will work with older Windows operating systems instead of demanding that you download the latest bloatware or update. As if this wasn't enough, you can also convert the music from your audio cassettes and old LPs to a digital format (this is a bonus feature as far as I'm concerned since the product is marketed as primarily a video product). I also liked the fact that you can export the saved file to iTunes and, once ready, can view an old video you made years ago on your iPhone or iPad!

My only quibble is that the editing features aren't as extensive as those programs specifically made for enhancing your old videos, but overall the program provides everything you need to make a smooth transition from copying an old VHS to DVD. Overall I am very happy with this product.
text_fidelity_b: VIDBOX Video Conversion Suite

text_fidelity_a:
Waterproof Bone Conduction Headphones, IPX8 Waterproof 32GB Swimming MP3 Player Headphones Wireless Bluetooth 5.3 Open-ear Headphones with Mic for Swimming Skiing Cycling Driving Gym Workout(Black) PROS

1. These headphones are really different in appearance from regular earbud-type headphones, but they are oddly attractive in their design.

2. They are great for swimming in a pool or in any outdoor body of water, because they are extensively waterproof. They can be submerged to a depth of 20 meters (65 feet). This means they can be used for snorkeling and scuba diving.

3. They do not fit in the ear. Instead, sound is conducted through the cheekbone. I don’t understand the science behind this, but it does work.

4. They have the ability to play audio files from a built-in 32GB memory card.

5. When not submerged in water, they have Bluetooth capability. When underwater, you have to use the built-in memory card.

6. This type of headphones are outstanding for safety purposes. People who walk, jog or run on public sidewalks or, especially, on deserted park paths/trails, are taking a big risk if they have their ears plugged with regular Bluetooth earbuds such that are not aware of sounds around them that could signal danger (e.g., a bike speeding down the park trail, careless skaters or skateboarders sharing the sidewalk and, worst of all, muggers).

6. A built-in microphone allows you to use the Bluetooth function to place and received calls on your cell phone.

7. These headphones are lightweight, durable, and flexible.

CONS

1. Other than for water sports and for safety purposes, these headphones are not as good as regular earbuds, because their sound quality is comparatively quite inferior.

2. Compared to regular Bluetooth earbuds, their price is very high.
text_fidelity_b: Waterproof Bone Conduction Headphones, IPX8 Waterproof 32GB Swimming MP3 Player Headphones Wireless Bluetooth 5.3 Open-ear Headphones with Mic for Swimming Skiing Cycling Driving Gym Workout(Black)

text_fidelity_a:
Pioneer SP-BS22-LR Andrew Jones Home Audio Bookshelf Loudspeakers (Set of 2) If you're like me, you've done some research (extensively in my case) on comparing these two speakers, and have probably come out with a vague case for each of them. Some prefer the Miccas, some prefer the Pioneers. I decided to order both and find out what the deal is for myself. And although I haven't ordered many speakers, I've been a headphone enthusiast for many years.

FYI, I'm using these with a sub (Dayton 1200), so I can't comment on their performance by themselves.

The Miccas sound pretty good, with clear highs - solid performers for movies. But they never made me very impressed by their sound. They seem serviceable, good for the price but not particularly great. They are by no means a bad speaker, but they are a bit thin sounding, kind of one-note.

With the Miccas, if felt like I was listening to music, but with the Pioneers, I felt like I was feeling it. They have a lush tone that is very musical, and I noticed I was bobbing my head to some songs I wasn't before. Better dynamics, soundstage - they really allow you to get lost in the music. Even though the driver size is the same, everything sounds bigger, with more depth.

And even though they have less treble energy than the MB42X, they seem to retrieve a bit more detail. Certainly not "veiled", just darker in tone. I'd prefer there to be slightly less treble than too much - just make sure to remove the grill, as it can make them slightly too dark.

For $20 extra bucks currently I think it's a no-brainer to get the Pioneers, unless you can't particularly stand speakers on the warmer side. I have the center channel coming in today - I've heard mixed reports on it, but if it's anything like the bookshelves I'm sure I'll be satisfied.
text_fidelity_b: Pioneer SP-BS22-LR Andrew Jones Home Audio Bookshelf Loudspeakers (Set of 2)

text_fidelity_a:
Toshiba TransMemory Pro USB 3.0 Flash Drive (PFU064U-1BDS) With its huge 64GB file storage capacity, this flash drive can theoretically store the entire contents of a PC's hard drive and its operating system. Since I don't have that many files to store on an everyday basis, I am reserving this flash drive to store high-resolution videos and other RAM-eating monster files.

For $80, this is rather overpriced. There are USB drives that are cheaper and will do the job just as well. To make the USB look like it's worth the extra price, Toshiba made the casing unnecessarily oversized - there's no practical reason why the USB case had to be so wide (you will have trouble sticking another USB drive next to it, which is annoying). It's a gimmick to impress the user, nothing more. However, when you hold it in your hand, it's not as heavy as the metallic finish would lead you to believe - it's actually very lightweight, and to be honest, feels cheap. I have questions of its durability, despite the fancy advertising.

To test, I copied all the videos I had stored in my PC to see how fast it would be to store all of them on this monster drive. I was disappointed that the saving time was not noticeably faster, which may not be the fault of the USB drive but rather my computer. However, I have to say it was a relief that I never got the "you don't have enough memory" message, so you can count on this USB to store tons of videos you can't find room for elsewhere.

The only drawback to this single-USB method of storage is that I don't feel entirely comfortable saving so much stuff on just ONE drive, despite its capacity. It's equivalent to putting all your eggs in one basket - what if you lose that single USB - you're screwed. Though convenient, I'd rather spread out my back-up files, so if you use this USB to save a huge file, I'd buy more than one just to be safe.

The other thing I thought was unnecessary was the included encryption software that's included on the drive. You only see it when you open up the Files folder, and there are two lengthy PDFs with instructions on how to activate the password and security options. Fortunately you do not require to activate them in order to use the drive - I've never found I needed such security measures, but if you plan to store financial data on this USB, it's a good feature.

Lastly, I hate the fact that, unlike my other drives, it has a cap. I am forever losing the caps to my flash drives and have since opted to buy only the retractable ones, where you can slide the connector in or out. Too bad this one doesn't have it, otherwise I would have added a star.

So, in short, a mixed review. Give me a drive that's cheaper, that's big on the inside but small on the outside, capless, and I'd buy more of them.
text_fidelity_b: Toshiba TransMemory Pro USB 3.0 Flash Drive (PFU064U-1BDS)

text_fidelity_a:
Creative Sound Blaster Roar 2 Portable NFC Bluetooth Speaker with aptX/AAC (Black) I’m a big fan of the Roar since it provides me with two key benefits: great sound and is easy to use. The Roar 2 retains those two benefits and adds one more: a smaller footprint. I’m going to try my best to not overuse the words “outstanding” and "impressive" in this review, but it’s going to be a challenge. This is an impressive speaker.

The out-of-the-box experience is nicely done. As expected at this price point, it comes in upscale packaging. More important, it comes with a pretty decent user guide. That’s significant since the Roar 2 has a lot of features – to call it just “a speaker” really shortchanges it. It’s also a recorder, a power bank, an MP3 player, an SD card reader, a speakerphone – it will even lull you to sleep with Bedtime Mode where it gradually decreases the volume and then powers off. My only complaint about the manual is that it’s physically small, which means the type size is also small. I do wish manufacturers would realize that those of us with aging eyes still like loud music!

And loud music is this product’s forte. I’m able to get room-filling sound while maintaining crisp highs, clear midrange and solid but not muddy bass. I can even go past room-filling to the “let’s annoy the neighbors” levels and still maintain impressive fidelity. Using the Tera Bass option boosts the bass response to the point where you would swear there was a separate subwoofer on the floor. You can see the end plates resonate to help drive the bass (plus it just looks really cool as well).

Day to day usage of the Roar 2 is straightforward even though there are so many features. All the buttons are labeled fairly clearly, albeit at times with small type. I would also have preferred a greater contrast to the labels since sometimes they are hard to see unless the Roar 2 is under a bright light. There are voice prompts for many key features which I found helpful. Normally I don’t care for voice prompts, but these were done in a natural sounding voice at a low volume making them not at all irritating. But, if you don’t like them at all, you can turn them off. There are small, but clear indicator lights to keep you apprised of battery charge level, settings, and other criteria.

The build quality is excellent. This feels as good as it looks, with a solid heft to it, an excellent quality metal grill, and quality plastic case components. All the buttons have a good tactile feel to them. I have it in white, which looks very nice with the gray contrast control pad. My only quibble is that some of the buttons/levers are on the small side. However, those tend to be the lesser used function. The main function buttons (on/off, volume, pairing, Tera Bass, etc.) are larger and easy to use.

The Roar 2 is not inexpensive, but the performance, build quality and features make it an excellent value. If you enjoy great sound and need to keep to a small footprint speaker, these should absolutely be on your short list (and at the top of it by a wide margin). Highly, highly recommend.
[Sample provided for review]
text_fidelity_b: Creative Sound Blaster Roar 2 Portable NFC Bluetooth Speaker with aptX/AAC (Black)

I do my web surfing on a tablet or a laptop and I use my phone mostly for texting and holding music files. Given that my biggest complaint was that my 5 year old Android phone running version 4.4 of KitKat was limited to a 32GB SD card. At least that was the accepted wisdom. Turns out there is a work around. The 32 GB was ok for MP3’s but sucked for hi-res flac’s which my phone will play. Turns out that if you use a third party formatting software (I used Rufus 3.1) and format your card as a FAT32 as opposed to the Windows default exFAT you can load up a couple thousand 16 or 24bit flac’s on a 128GB card and it works just fine. So my old dinosaur phone has lots of life left in it.

text_fidelity_a:
JVC HARX700 Precision Sound Full Size Headphones - Black I own the HARX900 (2 pairs) and got these as laptop headphones. I connect these to a USB DAC and can really get good sound with the laptop's EQ and the DAC pushing the voltage. These aren't too heavy for my head, have a comfy band and, most important of all, they don't mess with my glasses or press my ears into the glasses. Fully closed headphones tend to be too tight around the ears for glasses and open types have too much sound bleed and environmental intrusion so this semi-closed design is wonderful for me. The 50mm drivers pump tons of good sound and, if you have the right hardware, these sound excellent even at lower volumes. The sound is very balanced and isn't super bass heavy. These are good for jazz, rock, spoken word, and just about anything else. I enjoy the longer cord because I can run this into a mic jack behind a desktop PC and still have plenty of slack. At 48ohms, these take a little more to push than the regular 32ohm cans, but most cell phones will still sound great with these.

The only bad thing is that the pleather ear pads WILL degrade after a couple of years of constant usage and there aren't really any easy ways to replace them. You buy at your own risk in the aftermarket world, but if you can locate a good source of earpads, these are worth keeping for the long haul once you've burned them in. They sound just as good for most applications as the HARX900 and you will want to get a pair for home and for the office.
text_fidelity_b: JVC HARX700 Precision Sound Full Size Headphones - Black

text_fidelity_a:
Kindle Fire - Includes Special Offers (Previous Generation - 2nd) I just received my kindle fire today. I had a hard time deciding between the HD, this, and the paperwhite. I decided on this one, because I really thought I'd like the immersion reading. I have an audible account and I've been reading along to the audiobooks. It's amazing how fast I can get through the books (at 3x speed) and I really retain the info. The immersion reading is super-easy to use and definitely worth upgrading to this. The whole point of the kindle is to read more, and this new feature makes it possible to read 2 or 3 times as many books in the same amount of time. I'm an average-speed reader and was able to read 4 books (with the help of the audiobook reading pace) in the last 30 days and one was the 800+ page Stephen king, "11/22/63".

I also tested out the text to speech. It's a lady's voice and much, much, easier to understand than the text to speech on my kindle keyboard. It also has many speed options and I think it reads faster than my kindle keyboard version. I am very, very pleased with it.

It is much more responsive than the previous kindle fire I'm upgrading from.

If you are worried about the free offers, don't be. I DETEST commercials and advertising so much, I quit reading magazines and watching television. The offers only show on the startup, no big deal. I already took advantage of a $5.00 credit for amazon video. I was able to rent two movies and it only cost me 89 cents, when it was said and done, and I was planning on renting Hunger Games tonight, anyway. So, so far, I don't mind the offers at all.

My favorite feature is the immersion reading and the text-to-speech improvements. I also downloaded all the free kindle books with the free audiobooks for the immersion experience. These are books I always wanted to read,but never had the discipline to just read them. Reading and listening to those books are worth the price of this new gadget, IMO.

Way to go, Amazon, for a great product and a great price!

P.S.
I have an iPad, and the last time I went on vacation, I left it at home and brought only my fire and kindle keyboard. I didn't miss my iPad at all and this new gen fire is even better. Seriously, it's that good.
text_fidelity_b: Kindle Fire - Includes Special Offers (Previous Generation - 2nd)

Kinivo BTH220 Bluetooth Stereo Headphone – Supports Wireless Music Streaming and Hands-Free Calling I needed a cheap pair of bluetooth headphones for my Nexus for traveling, but didn't want to make too many compromises in favor of cost. These turned out quite well.

I was concerned about other reviews noting that the one-size-fits-all aspect of these headphones might be a problem with those with larger noggins (I am one of those people), but did not have any difficultly wearing these headphones - it fits with room to spare and parks securely around my ears.

The sound is decent - better than I expected given the price. I like that you can make volume adjustments with a push of a button on the right-ear side.

The headphones recharge via a USB port to your computer (or use the USB on any plug adapter that you may have for your other devices -- I used my Amazon Kindle plug adapter), with an indicator light changing from red to blue when it is fully charged. I'm not sure of the total battery life, but I've used them for six hours in a single stretch, and they still were going strong.

I also tried walking around and away from my Nexus 7, and the headphones still worked fine. I didn't test the absolute limit of its range, but I got a good 20 feet away on the same floor without a problem.

The sound and build quality won't knock your socks off, but for the price, it's a great performer. Definitely recommend this as if you're looking for a good value in a bluetooth headphone.

text_fidelity_a: VIZIO M70-C3 70-Inch Class Ultra HD Full-Array LED Smart TV I really like this TV. So why 4 stars instead of 5? Well let me start with what is great about this TV and then we will get into why I dropped it a star. The price is amazing of course. I think back to the 42 inch Panasonic Plasma that I bought in 2002 and cringe at the multiple thousands spent. This is a lot of TV for the money. The picture is great. We have a 2012 59 inch top of the line Samsung Plasma and the picture on the Vizio is quite a bit sharper and brighter. It has replaced the Samsung as our go to Blue Ray movie night TV. So to this point we have a TV that is well priced and provides a great picture. So lets move on to the bad. Viewing angle. In our living room a couch sits directly in front of the Vizio. From the couch the picture is AMAZING. Off at about a 35 degree angle sits a recliner and the picture loses a lot of color, brightness and sharpness as viewed from the chair. It is not a horrible picture from the chair but it is quite a difference from straight on. The other is the somewhat slow response from the Vizio smart TV system. Compared to hooking up a Roku the initial start up and response is much slower. Of course if you are going to hook up a Roku then this is no big deal. If you do not have viewing angle concerns and are hooking up a Roku then I think you will absolutely love this amazing bargain.
text_fidelity_b: VIZIO M70-C3 70-Inch Class Ultra HD Full-Array LED Smart TV

text_fidelity_a:
Kikkerland UL03-A Universal Travel Adapter, Black I ended up returning these. I'm going to France and the UK, which have different plug styles. I thought this would be a pretty cool way to get an adapter for each country in one neat little gadget. Well, it looks like it would work fine, but it's twice as big as a standard simple one-piece adapter. So, for size and weight, it works out the same as having a simple adapter for France and a simple adapter for the UK. And it's more than twice the price of two simple adapters, so for price it's worse. Independent of price, it doesn't make sense to me to have something complicated when there aren't any advantages over the simple solution. I'm concerned that the complexity just adds more ways for something to go wrong, and the last thing you want to do on a trip is add more ways for something to go wrong.

So, I don't think this product makes any sense if you just need on or two plug styles. However, you would start seeing a benefit if you need three or more different plug styles on your trip.
text_fidelity_b: Kikkerland UL03-A Universal Travel Adapter, Black

Lexar JumpDrive S35 64GB USB 3.0 Flash Drive - LJDS35-64GABNL (Assorted colors) This jumpdrive is USB 3.0 (fast) but backward compatible with 2.0. It's a little cheesy looking because of its plastic "bubblegum" look, but the color-coding of the different size drives could be useful. I got the bright green 32 GB USB 3.0 stick for review, and when I put it into my USB port it showed installation files on the drive for both Windows and Mac. I double-clicked the Mac for my MacBook Pro, and it presented me with the installation screens. It was a little confusing how to get the software installed, and initially I had to install it on my computer to access the installation for just the flash drive; it's supposed to be optional to install it on your computer, but it wasn't apparent how to bypass computer installation. I had to delete my computer vault after it was created to get it off my computer.

Another confusion is that you are taken to a website with an offer for an Encryptstick software upgrade for a reduced cost or free for a 14-day trial. Apparently, all the best features of this device are not available if you just use the stick as a USB drive with the standard "Encryptstick Lite" app that comes with it. You will have AES encryption, but not the "military grade encryption," whatever that means. (The website lists the option to encrypt vaults with 128, 256, or 512-bit AES ciphers [1024-bit coming], registered and government approved, FIPS 140-2 compliant). Here are the other features listed on the website and, again, it's not clear which come with the standard installation and which with the upgraded one:

Runs on Multiple OS computers and all recently made USB flash drives
Encrypt & Decrypt Your Private Files
Easy to Use Encryption Interface [debatable!]
Speedy Auto-Updater
Lost Flash Drive Data Recovery Feature
Advanced Virtual Keyboard
Lock out Computer Installation is Optional - Not Essential
Lock out No Admin Rights Required
File Wipe Instant Lock
Quick Search, Live Search
Automatic Timeout
Limited Login Attempts
File Wipe File Shredder

I went on and purchased the upgrade (12.99 to Lexar users instead of the usual 39.99) because the advanced backup features are only available with the upgraded version and I did want them, but I thought it was a little sneaky how they presented all this. It's really not clear that you don't have to get the upgrade to make the stick itself work. Once you've purchased the upgrade, you are given links to download the upgrade for all versions (PC, Mac, and Linux) in an email.

Somehow I wound up with both the EncryptStick Lite and EncryptStick apps both running at the same time. I could not close out of either one of them, and attempting to eject the jumpdrive gave me an error saying I needed to close out of both apps. I had to force-quit the Lite app. That made me nervous about the whole thing.

I have to mention the following experience because, for me, it was an issue. The little lanyard (about the length of the drive when installed) is not attached when you take it out of the package, and I had a heck of a time getting it threaded through the end. The cord won't bend through the jumpdrive's hole, so it requires using an implement of some come to grasp the thread end and pull it through. My tweezers were too large, and so was the end of the large paperclip (all I had), so I wound up having to strip off the coating on an old bobby pin that I just happened to have lying in a drawer. Even then, I had to pop up part of the plastic cover on the front of the drive case a little to work the thread through, and I was worried about destroying the drive in the process. This whole process was very aggravating, so I think it would be better if they sold these with the lanyard already attached. Customers can then remove it if they don't want it, but I think the lanyard is quite useful. If you have more than one of these drives, you could hang them all up on a keyholder at your desk, then pull one off to take with you as needed.

Please note that I am downrating this product because of the initial confusion and hassles above, although in fairness this is not a good indication of the reliability and performance of the jumpdrive once the software and lanyard are installed. Consider this review to be of the initial experience with the jumpdrive and software. If I discover any more problems as I use this drive over time, I will come back and post them. For now, though, I'm tired of fooling with it!
text_fidelity_b: Lexar JumpDrive S35 64GB USB 3.0 Flash Drive - LJDS35-64GABNL (Assorted colors)

LeeKooLuu Backup Camera Rear View Monitor Kit HD 1080P for Car Truck Minivan Waterproof Night Vision DIY Grid Lines LK3 The camera and kit are a superb value. Installation was not difficult (including BOTH TIMES, I had to install the cable). Let me explain: When ordering it doesn't tell you what size cable comes with it, which is a 23 ft. cable. I found this out the hard and dirty way after a couple of hours on a winter Sunday afternoon painstakingly dragging myself underneath my truck; routing, securing, and cable-tying the camera cable from the back of my 2009 Ram 1500 (crew cab short bed) to the front, just to find out when I went to bring it through the firewall, I was about 5-7ft too short to reach the middle of my trucks console and mounting location. Pretty frustrating after spending hours to install and come up short. On re-reading the instructions by LKL they advised 'if cable too short, contact us for the longer 33ft. or 50ft cable'. Uhm OK, and I sent an email, and to their credit, they responded within a couple of hours asking for the size I wanted that would work. Unfortunately, a "short splicer" cable wasn't an option with both male finish end couplers on their cables to simply "Splice" into what was already routed 95% of the way already, so I asked for the 33ft. one. They sent it immediately, and I got it a few days later with plans to complete installation the following weekend from my original effort. So, new cable in hand I had to re-route the new cable basically starting over. A bit frustrating BUT hopefully this post will change their ordering system to ask "cable size" based upon application upfront; like for a car. SUV, truck, or RV. If, not simply message them ahead of time to install to see if they can send you a longer cable. not as efficient, but will save you the double-install time.

That said, I really like my camera. It has great clarity, good screen size, and detail. I like the flexible options for 16:9 vs. Narrower field, grid options and adjustments, etc. I also recommend adding LED back up lights to improve the night view of the camera which already includes some LEDs to help with night safety (you are likely reading this because you want better safety, and rearview vision, especially at night, correct?) You will already be removing one taillight assembly installing the splice-in to power the camera with the backup light wire, so you might as well install LED Backup bulbs both sides of the taillamp assembly.

I had a perfect spot in mind to install my camera in the center on top of my dash above the radio into a little "coin tray" recess. I had to snip about a half-inch off the camera holder base front and back to make it nestle in the bottom and adhere with the provided mounting tap securely. If I had it to do over again I likely would get their wireless camera product first, then see if the wireless signal worked OK given the length of the truck. (They don't recommend their wireless version for larger vehicles, like full-sized SUV's, trucks, or RV's but reviewers have reported satisfactory results with trucks and SUVs) Although it's a bit more $$ for wireless the amount of install time required for do-it-yourselfer's, or professional installation would be well worth it. If the wireless signal isn't good enough, return it since it wouldn't have been installed fully; then just order up this wired option. Good luck and happy backing up!
text_fidelity_b: LeeKooLuu Backup Camera Rear View Monitor Kit HD 1080P for Car Truck Minivan Waterproof Night Vision DIY Grid Lines LK3

text_fidelity_a:
Samsung Chromebook (Wi-Fi, 11.6-Inch) 2012 Model I wanted a computer that was fast and efficient, and didn't bother me with updates all the time. I wanted a device with a keyboard that I could use to surf the Internet, check email, type documents, create to-do lists, update my calendar, and complete quick calculations. I've found all of that and more with Chromebook.

Now, as other reviewers have mentioned, the learning curve might be just a bit steep for those unused to Google's products (besides their search engine, of course). But I'm telling you, once you get the hang of using Google Docs for typing documents, Google slides for creating presentations, Google Calendar for setting dates, etc., you will not want to go back. If you lose your Chromebook or find yourself without it, you can go onto any device that connects to the Internet and find your documents, presentation, calendar, etc.

Technically, you don't even need a Chromebook to use those products, just a Google account. But then you wouldn't have such an efficient, fast machine to use them on--and why would you ever want that?

---------

Just a couple notes on the downsides:

1. Printing is an issue if you don't have a "Cloud Print Ready" printer. Since I don't, my computer scientist husband had to find a work-around.

2. You cannot download external programs. I have to keep my old laptop around for when I want to use iTunes, Blackboard IM (for school), and my scanner. To me, it's no big deal, but don't think that you can use Chromebook for everything because you simply can't. To me, the pros completely outweigh the cons!
text_fidelity_b: Samsung Chromebook (Wi-Fi, 11.6-Inch) 2012 Model

text_fidelity_a:
Sony Xperia Ear Duo True Wireless headset – Black EDIT: Sony sent me a replacement unit under warranty because of the broken charger. The new unit works as advertised, so I'm upgrading my review to 3 stars. Some users may rate this more highly because of your needs. I give it 3 stars because they are difficult to use, uncomfortable to wear, have mediocre battery life, and are very expensive.

I wanted to give these a fair and thorough test, but unfortunately quality seems to be lacking and it died after just 2 days. First, the rubber ear tip on the right side kept falling off every time I took the earpiece out. Maybe I'm clumsy or maybe it is too fragile, but either way this is really annoying. Second, the battery life is terrible. The battery life indicator dropped from 70% to 30% after just 20 minutes of listening to music. Finally, the charger died. One of the little pins that connected the charger device to the earpiece broke off (or never was attached). Without it, I cannot recharge the right earpiece and since this is a non-standard charger, the whole thing is now useless.

Even if the headphones were 100% functional, here are some general thoughts:
1. Sound quality is very good for headphones that allow you to hear your surroundings. I don't have to take the headphones off to talk to someone standing next to me.
2. That is great because getting these things on or off is much more cumbersome than any other headphone I have ever tried.
3. The user manual really wants you to control these things using finger and head gestures. Maybe my memory is poor, but I can never remember all those things. Even when I'm reading the manual and trying to use the gestures, half the time they don't work.
4. This headset is expensive if all you can do is listen to music and phone calls. They are heavily advertising the "personal assistant" feature as well. The personal assistant feature asks for all kinds of permissions so it can read your messages and emails to you. After the recent Facebook hack, I am really reluctant to grant all these permissions.
5. The personal assistant works best if you have the headphones on all the time instead of just occasionally when you listen to music. However, the advertised battery life of these headphones is only 2-4 hours and my experience is less than that. Constantly recharging these things is a real hassle. Even taking them on and off several times a day is a real hassle.
6. The headphones are cumbersome to take on and off and wear and they are cumbersome entirely because they want to remove the wire between the 2 sides that cheaper headsets have. I don't think that tradeoff is worthwhile if you're not wearing these constantly and you can't wear them constantly because of the battery life.
text_fidelity_b: Sony Xperia Ear Duo True Wireless headset – Black

The tilt feature is very nice.  Installation was simple enough; I didn't have a stud where I wanted it, so fixed a piece of finished wood about an inch bigger in all dimensions than the wall-mount bracket using drywall anchors, then screwed the arm to that.  Leveling was simple, the bottom hole is elongated to allow some adjustments.  The torpedo level magnet sticks to the arm, so you have both hands free to make sure the arm is level, tightenign the screw with one hand while applying whatever push is needed to keep the arm level until the bottom screw is tight.  The allen-wrench that comes with the bag of screws can be used to tighten or loosen the adjustment screws at the shoulder/elbow/wrist, but I didn't need to use it.  The adjustments were tight enough and didn't move once the monitor was where I wanted it.  The two big screws to hold it to the wall are black, but the small screws that hold the monitor to the arm (they come with the kit) are silver-colored rather than black; so the monitor is black, and the arm is black, but the screws are metal color.  But who looks at the back of the thing?  I'd buy another any time.
